title: Vinted Suspended Me for "Commercial Selling" — What the 5-Day Ban Means and How to Appeal
intro: A "commercial selling" restriction means Vinted has decided your account looks like a business rather than someone passing on their own things. It normally arrives as a temporary selling ban — sellers describe five days first, then seven, then a permanent block — with some or all of your listings hidden and a message telling you to remove "commercial" listings or move to a Pro account. You can appeal it once, using the link in that moderation message, and the appeals that get overturned are built on proof of where the items came from, not on arguing about how much you sell.
meta_description: Vinted "commercial selling" ban: why the 5-day restriction hits, what triggers it, the 7-day and permanent escalation, and the appeal evidence that works.
author: Supervint Team
cta_text: Get alerted the moment genuine items are listed

body.heading: What the message actually says
paragraphs: The notice is oddly vague for something that stops you selling. Vinted says your account has been restricted for commercial selling, that specific listings have been hidden, and that you should remove the commercial listings or convert to a Pro account. What it rarely says is which signal tipped it over — which is why the same question appears on r/vinted and r/vintedUK most weeks: "I'm not a business, so why am I banned?"

The shape of the story is almost identical each time. Someone who has been listing for months gets a five-day selling ban out of nowhere. Their listings go invisible. They appeal, confirm they're a private seller, attach photos of the boxes the items came out of, and get a generic reply upholding the decision — often quoting the line that uploading listings for resale isn't allowed — plus a suggestion to upgrade to Pro.

What makes it feel arbitrary is how small the trigger looks. Sellers describe single cheap high-street items being the listing that got hidden, and one seller clearing a family member's old jewellery — eighteen pieces at a few pounds each — got the same five-day ban.

body.heading: The rule underneath the message
paragraphs: Vinted's Catalog Rules are explicit. Section 4 says: "Standard Vinted accounts are for private, non-commercial use only. As a standard seller, you can't use Vinted to operate a reselling business (even if you own a legally registered business), or act as a professional sole trader."

The Help Centre article on commercial selling fills in the detail: standard accounts can't be used to sell professionally, "including buying or sourcing items and reselling them at a profit". It does carve out the case most people are actually in — brand-new personal items such as gifts or purchases that didn't fit are allowed "as long as you originally bought or acquired them for your own personal use".

Vinted's own Trust & Safety lead has said publicly that volume isn't the test: "Selling a lot doesn't make you a business. If you've had a huge clear-out and you're listing two hundred items from your own wardrobe, that's completely fine." The line, according to Vinted, is intent.

Intent isn't something a detection system can see. Vinted describes enforcement as a mix of "trained moderation teams, member reports and detection tools", looking at a member's "behaviour", "listing patterns" and "account history", and says it doesn't publish how those signals are weighted. You're judged on the pattern your account makes — and a large clear-out done quickly makes the same pattern as a reseller.

body.heading: The escalation ladder sellers keep describing
paragraphs: This is the part that scares people, and it appears across separate threads from different accounts: the restriction escalates. Five days first. Then seven, if you carry on listing the same way. Then, sometimes, a permanent ban.

One seller described exactly that sequence — five days for suspected commercial reselling, then seven with an instruction to remove the suspected items or face a permanent ban, then a permanent ban after they complied. Another reported a five-day ban months earlier and a seven-day ban on the day of posting.

Vinted's Catalog Rules allow for it. The penalties section says that where a member repeatedly uploads prohibited items or "items of a seemingly commercial nature", Vinted "can suspend their account (e.g. for a period of 7 days) or even block it definitively" depending on severity. The seven-day step isn't a rumour; it's written in as an example.

There's a trap in the middle of it: the message tells you to remove the commercial listings, but sellers report they can't edit or delete them while the restriction is active. Wait it out, then remove them the moment you can get back in — and pause paid bumps, because hidden listings still take the money without being visible to buyers.

body.heading: What seems to trigger the flag
paragraphs: Nobody outside Vinted can say which signal fired, but the patterns in the threads are consistent. Listing pace comes up most: sellers who got flagged describe uploading two to five items a day, or seven to eight a day, or around seventy items over two months. The advice from people who've been through it is blunt: slow down, and don't list a run of near-identical items back to back.

New condition labels draw attention. The rule is about new stock bought to resell, but detection appears to lean on items marked new with tags or new without tags, and on multiples of similar new pieces. Description style matters too: several sellers had copy that read like shop copy — "add a pop of colour to your wardrobe" — and the replies agreed that's exactly what the system looks for. Same for templated or AI-generated descriptions and reused photos.

Buying to resell is the clearest breach. Sellers describe sourcing from charity shops, or buying cheaply on Vinted itself and relisting for profit, then being unsurprised when the restriction lands. That is commercial activity under Vinted's own definition, whatever the volume. Member reports feed the same system, and sellers who have pulled their account data describe clusters of reports arriving together.

body.heading: How to build an appeal that actually gets read
paragraphs: The mechanics are fixed. Vinted's Contacts for dispute resolution page says that if action has been taken against your account or listings and you believe it's wrong, you appeal using the link in the inbox message or email containing the moderation decision. Appeals must be made within six months, and a decision can only be appealed once. Vinted's Trust & Safety lead says each appeal gets manual review by a person on that team, and mistakes are reversed — which is why the content matters.

The appeals sellers describe as successful were evidence-heavy and specific about ownership: photos of the clothes stored for sale, the wardrobe they came from, and screenshots showing many items had originally been bought on Vinted, plus an explanation that the volume came from a complete wardrobe change. It went in once, in the same conversation, and the account was restored around fourteen days later.

The appeals that fail assert innocence instead of documenting it. Ticking "I'm a private seller" and attaching a photo of storage boxes, without tying each flagged listing to where it came from, got one seller a fast copy-paste rejection. The difference is whether the reviewer can match your explanation to the listings that were hidden.

So build the appeal around those specific listings. For each one, say where it came from and when, and attach the receipt, order confirmation, Vinted purchase history or photo that proves it. Keep it calm, factual and in one message, and don't argue the rule is unfair — the reviewer decides only whether the decision was correctly applied.

If it's rejected by what looks like a template and you have real evidence it was wrong, the escalation route is Vinted's legal team at legal@vinted.com, the address listed on Vinted's own Contacts for dispute resolution page for legal and regulatory issues. Sellers report getting a human reply that way, including one Pro seller told the commercial selling notice was a reminder rather than a decision.

body.heading: Does going Pro stop it, and what changes afterwards
paragraphs: Partly, and less than the message implies. Vinted Pro is free and, per Vinted, currently available in France, Italy, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and the UK, for sole traders, charities and registered businesses there. If Pro isn't available where you are, the Help Centre is clear you aren't allowed to sell as a business at all — so "just go Pro" isn't an option for everyone being told to do it.

Pro does not unlock new-item selling. Vinted's own explanation is that Pro members can sell as a business but must still only sell second-hand items, and that selling mostly new items, or multiples of the same new item, isn't allowed whether that's commercial stock, bulk-bought or drop-shipped. Pro sellers also take on obligations private sellers don't, including a 14-day refund window. And Pro accounts get caught too: sellers describe the same notice on accounts already set up as Pro.
When the restriction lifts, change the pattern before you list again: space uploads out, write your own descriptions, photograph each item yourself, and avoid runs of near-identical new items.

Don't relabel genuinely new items as used to dodge the flag. Vinted's commercial selling guidance explicitly prohibits "listing new items as second-hand", and misrepresenting condition is a separate breach — you'd trade a temporary restriction for a stronger case. Keep your proof of where things came from before you need it.

faq.question: Why did Vinted flag me for commercial selling when I'm not a business?
faq.answer: Because the rule is about intent but the detection works on patterns. Vinted's Catalog Rules limit standard accounts to private, non-commercial use, which its Help Centre defines as not buying or sourcing items to resell at a profit. Vinted's own Trust & Safety lead has said selling a lot doesn't make you a business — listing two hundred items from your own wardrobe is fine — but a fast run of similar or new-with-tags listings looks the same to an automated system as a reseller does.

faq.question: How long does a Vinted commercial selling ban last?
faq.answer: Sellers consistently describe five days for a first restriction, seven days for a second, and a permanent ban after that if the pattern continues. Vinted's Catalog Rules support this: the penalties section says repeated prohibited items or items of a seemingly commercial nature can lead to a suspension "e.g. for a period of 7 days" or a definitive block depending on severity.

faq.question: Can I delete or edit the hidden listings during the ban?
faq.answer: Sellers report that you usually can't — the message tells you to remove the commercial listings, but editing and deleting are disabled while the restriction is active. The workaround described in the threads is to wait for the ban to lift and remove them immediately afterwards, and to pause paid bumps so you're not paying to promote invisible listings.

faq.question: What evidence gets a commercial selling appeal accepted?
faq.answer: Proof of where each flagged item came from. Sellers whose appeals succeeded attached photos of the wardrobe and the boxes the items were stored in, plus screenshots showing that items being resold had originally been bought on Vinted, and explained why the upload volume was unusually high. Submit it once through the appeal link in the moderation message and keep it factual.

faq.question: Does upgrading to Vinted Pro stop commercial selling bans?
faq.answer: No. Pro lets you sell as a business where the programme is available, but Vinted still requires Pro sellers to sell second-hand items only and prohibits selling mostly new items or multiples of the same new item. Pro accounts report receiving the same commercial selling notice, and Pro brings extra obligations such as a 14-day refund window.

faq.question: How many times can I appeal a Vinted moderation decision?
faq.answer: Once, and within six months. Vinted's Contacts for dispute resolution page states that appeals must be made within six months of receiving the moderation decision and that a decision can only be appealed once. Each appeal is reviewed manually, so make the single appeal complete rather than sending several partial ones.
